newsitem.title: USA: NAIRU skeptic Greenspan seen holding rates steady.
newsitem.headline: NAIRU skeptic Greenspan seen holding rates steady.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, skeptical of claims that low unemployment causes inflation, is expected to argue against raising interest rates at a policy-making meeting this week, analysts said.

With economic growth slowing and inflation low, they said that Greenspan should have little trouble convincing fellow policymakers to hold off from tightening credit again at the two-day meeting that begins on Tuesday.
"I don't think they're going to do anything," American Stock Exchange Chairman and former Boston Fed President Richard Syron said.

Anti-inflation hawks at the Fed recognize that it would be difficult for the central bank to raise rates at a time of slowing growth. But they believe that higher rates will be needed eventually to keep inflation in check because the economy is already running above capacity.
At 4.8 percent, the unemployment rate is at its lowest in nearly 24 years and is well below levels that in the past have led to stepped-up wage demands and higher inflation.

However, Fed officials said that Greenspan is skeptical of such arguments, which are based on the concept of NAIRU -- the Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment. That theory contends that inflation picks if the unemployment rate falls below a certain level, the NAIRU.
"I want you to understand that a very substantial part of the academic community does believe that," Greenspan told lawmakers at a hearing in March. "I am very skeptical of that relationship myself."

The Fed chief believes that policymakers do not know what NAIRU is -- if indeed there is such a single rate -- and that they should instead look for signs of stresses and strains in the economy in deciding monetary policy, officials said.

"Alan Greenspan is downplaying NAIRU and upgrading actual inflation reports as well as commodity price indicators," said Lawrence Kudlow, chief economist of American Skandia Life Assurance Co in Connecticut.

Wages have picked up in response to the tightness of the labor market -- a fact that has not escaped Greenspan's notice. But Fed officials said that the central bank chief welcomes higher wages as long as they are matched by increased worker productivity, and thus are not inflationary.

In an interview earlier this month, Fed Vice Chair Alice Rivlin noted that corporate profits are holding up well, indicating that firms are not having trouble paying the higher wages, presumably because of increased productivity.

By some measures, inflation looks to have decelerated rather than accelerated in recent months. For the three months ended May, consumer prices rose at an annualized rate of just 0.8 percent. That compares with a 3.3 percent rise for all 1996.
"We've seen no evidence of any acceleration in inflation, White House chief economist and former Fed Governor Janet Yellen told reporters on Monday.
